questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Taiwan because I've always wanted to visit the Chinese speaking world, without actually going to China. I heard some rumours that trips to China could be at best cumbersome as a non-Mandarin speaking foreigner, and heard much nicer things about travelling to Hong Kong or Taiwan, and ended up choosing Taiwan. I did not end up regretting this choice at all.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The trip as a whole was wonderful. There were many moments of hair-pulling frustration, boxing with cumbersome bureaucracy, and a delayed full-scale pandemic response, but all of it paled in comparison to how stunning the nature was, how amazing it was to learn history and experience a completely different culture,  and how incredibly friendly the people there were. I didn't speak any Mandarin, but the locals all tried (and mostly failed) to learn English, so there was an understanding that really afforded you quite a bit of leeway to practice your charades. Taiwan is pretty excluded from the itenerarys of surrounding Asia backpackers, so all local tourist facilities are designed primarily for internal tourism. Outside of Taipei especially, you may be the first foreigner to stop by in a long while. It'll be great, I promise.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was pretty bad. It was definitely, DEFINITELY made worse by covid (keep in mind that this review is written in start 2023), but don't expect the consulates (de facto embassies) to go easy on you just because the regulation was loosened. Most students were given ultra-short 3-5 day deadlines to stamp maybe 5 different papers. The papers they send you on mail will probably not be the right ones. The ones they send you on mail will definitely not be sufficient. Many of the procedures can only be done in Mandarin, so make some Mandarin speaking friend before you leave, immediately upon arrival, or get very good at guessing what papers can safely be ignored and what are official papers that need immediate attention and probably a couple of stamps.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Very little. Most locals are culturally inclined to be incredibly helpful by nature, but dealing with bureacracy seems to be the one exception. Expect people to be annoyed with you for asking how to fill out a certain form. Expect people to be annoyed with you for not knowing where things are. Expect people to be annoyed with you for not knowing your chinese name. Expect registration to be minimum (1) full 40-work week, and plan that it may be twice that. I met people who were still dealing with their registration well 3-4 months into their stay.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Its frustrating.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was frustrating. Off campus is typically more expensive, and most landlords will try to scam you. You can, and probably should, get an English speaking landlord and English contracts, but expect to pay some hefty fees for the guarantee of not getting too ripped off.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Expect to pay rent a month in advance, and pay a 2 month deposit that you can get back at the end. This means you may need a hefty upfront investment to live off-campus. If you don't manage to find someone to take over your room by the end, you may legally be on the hook for rent until a replacement tenant is found. Plan to do things related to your accomodation well in advance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you do get housing on-campus, expect very socially conservative rules, strictly enforced. Male only dorms, female only dorms, strict hall-passes, no overnight visitors at threat of immediate expulsion, from the dorm and possibly from the school. The on campus dorms also get very, very cold in December. However, the social life tends to be better in the dorms than on-campus, although its perfectly possible to have a good social life if you rent privately.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Registration was a nightmare, and probably the single worst part of the entire process. The information on the NTU course website is borderline unreadable, a random mix of chinese symbols and short blurbs of google translated bits of text, often seemingly unrelated to the course at hand. 70-80% is just straight up a lie, maybe true somewhere in the early 2010s, or so generally inaccurate that it may as well be. The last 20-30% is probably true, but is written in such a cryptic way way that it may only make sense to you retroactively several months into your stay. Classes may be cancelled last minute. Classes that are listed as being in English may simply just have a lecturer that CAN speak english, although the actual course may be in Chinese. Courses' schedule may change last minute, so that all your classes end up lined up on the same day. I lined up 40 ECTS, and ended up only being able to take 22.5 ECTS. Plan accordingly.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was a 2 week drop-add period. This system supposedly alleviates the problems of the course website, but essentially entails that its near impossible for you to discern going into the period what classes you'll actually end up doing. My only recommendation is sign up for as many classes as possible, and then drop aggresively the bad ones, so you end up with a tolerable mix of classes.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Technically you could probably ask the office of international affairs, but I've found them to be not very helpful people on the whole. You're mostly on your own.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got some of the classes that I wanted, but one my core classes was dropped, and some of my classes turned out awful towards the end. Try to see what rumours that you can pick up on the 2 week window, as rumours tend to be a much better instruction than the website / what the instructors may tell you.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sign yourself up for as much as possible, and drop quickly. Its ok to drop halfway into the semester. Plan for the fact that many things may go wrong. Most host instutitions that I heard of were alright with you not doing a full 30 ECTS block, although it in some cases had implications for funding for scholarships (e.g. Danish SU).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was alright. I can't speak to the quality of the teaching in Mandarin, but most the English speaking classes went out of their way to be as inclusive to non-majors within their department as possible, as each department tended to only offer few actual English classes. This means that many of the classes couldn't actually require much background knowledge, and hence you will probably end up doing quite a few "introduction to ..."-type classes. Most of the professors for the English classes had an American Ivy League Ma/PhD, so the actual quality wasn't low, the problem was mainly just the target audience was very broad. There's also a HUGE gap in intensity between classes, where in some classes you may end up only studying 1-2 days for the entire semester, and some 2-3 weeks. Plan according to the trip that you want to have.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Most classes consisted entirely of lectures and a little bit of homework, i.e. there were no practice classes. You don't understand how much you miss practice classes until you don't have them. The lack of practice classes went hand-in-hand with a style of teaching where you're expected to remember the contents of the lectures verbatim, with many questions to homework/exams literally, number-for-number, having been presented as a .PPTX on the board a couple of weeks earlier. This style of teaching will be comfortable for some, and really grate others the wrong way.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1. "Financial Market and Derivatives" 3 credits
2. "Trade Theory" 3 credits
3. "Python Programming Foundation" 3 credits
4. "Causal Inference and Prediction in Econometrics" 2 credits

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Causal Inference and Prediction in Econometrics has a really wonderful instructor if you're into econometric proofs. Note that you should feel more-than-confident in your multivariate optimization, i.e. the cross between linear algebra and calculus III, otherwise you're in for a rude awakening in the second half of the course. Trade Theory is almost mandatory for econ majors, as the instructor is really sweet, and it really is an easy A, thats pretty interesting along the way. Financial Market and Deriatives is the hardest course here, and has a notorious instructor, that experienced quite a bit of personal turmoil alongside the semester which translated into quite a bit of abuse at the student body, so its a little hard to recommend. The python programming courses tend to be very fun and free-spirited, and can only recommend them.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You'll notice that Taiwan is heavily tariffed by the surrounding world, likely owing to the political situation with China. Therefore, especially food will in general be much more expensive than you think. Additionally, your accomodation is very unlikely to come with a kitchen of any use, so you'll likely be eating out for 3 meals of the day. This will add up. The trains for travelling inside the country are additionally more expensive than you think, and you will want to take them, because Taiwan is wonderful to travel in. You may also want to put money aside for picking up a (cheap) airplane-ticket to Vietnam/Thailand/Philippines/Japan when your exchange ends.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Most international brands (UNIQLO/IKEA/Sony) will probably be the same price as at home, maybe 5-10% cheaper at best. Local brands tend to be 40-50% cheaper than west Europe. Food adds up because of the kitchen situation.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The gossip: NTU, although its definitely not official policy, appears to intentionally or not segregate students by their approximate region. Foreigners from Europe, foreigners from UK/US/AUS/NZ, foreigners from ASEAN all seem to be _mostly_ put on separate floors of the dorm, separate chinese classes, and just in general somehow end up separated. Additionally, you may find it difficult, although not impossible, to meet local friends who are comfortable enough in their English to be able to speak it in a group setting. You will likely therefore end up in Taiwan hanging out with people mostly from your approximate geographic region. At times this will be very comfortable: You'll be in a very strange country very far from home, and its nice to hear some German speakers inviting you for Christmas. At other times, you may wonder why you travelled halfway around the world to hang out with people who usually live right up against you anyway. If you want to meet truly "international" friends, plan accordingly.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Literally everything was available, although only some will be in English. Go to club day, around the start of the semester, and you'll find literally hundreds of activities. Keep in mind that most of it will be in Mandarin, but if you bring a mandarin speaking friend, or just go to a pretty foreigner-friendly club in general, then you should have a great time. Met several people who did skateboarding, baking, photography, sports, travelling and so on. Reputedly, especially the "hiking groups", of which there should be several, tend to be very good places to meet new friends and experience Taiwan.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I'm personally a little useless for club-activities, but I went to go see close to a million temples and museums. Often just taking a friend into the mountains to go see a temple is a wonderful way to spend an afternoon. Afterwards, try to pick up on what's happening in Taipei: There's many festivals, concerts, street parties, pop-up nightmarkets, 2 EUR michelin-star food stands and novel activities in general always available, and seemingly never that far from where you are.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Taiwan really shines outside of its cities. Go to the hot spring, go on the hikes, rent a scooter on the islands, make new friends, anything is possible, and everything is pretty affordable. The weather is likely to be highly unpredictable, and may rain for several weeks in a row, so when the weather allows, be sure to grab the oppurtunity to leave Taipei, because you may not know when that chance appears again.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It will take a while. The initial bit of your trip may feel downright hostile while you're adjusting, but that feeling subsides after a couple of weeks. Afterwards, you'll find yourself wishing many of the conveniences of Taipei were availble at home, like the almost completely ubiqutous presence of cheap convenience stores and ridicolously cheap rental bikes.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Its much easier if you have an activity. The hiking clubs will have the lowest barrier for entry, although the sports clubs also tend to be very approachable. The foreigner bars (namely Another Brick & Revolver, and to some extent most of Ximen) will also be a good entry point.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Expect Taiwenese people to be very polite, and have some difficulty to speak up if they're dissatisfied with something. You may at times be commiting a massive social faux pas, although you may not realize it, because no-one will as much as acknowledge it. The language barrier is also REAL. People may, in 1-on-1 speak to you in perfect english, but may in a group setting, or after one beer, completely lose this ability. Plan accordingly.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The politeness is real. Especially outside of Taipei, people will be so polite that you may not even realize what's happening before someone invited you into their house and fed you a full dinner and drinks. Taiwan in general is also just very safe. I lived in comfortably the dodgiest part of Taipei, and still did I not even once feel unsafe walking the streets alone at night, even when exploring dark unlit alleyways. There was a in one of my classes who got in a minor scooter-tuffle with a local, and it made national news and there was an interview and everything. It was really very minor. Taiwan is really very safe.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Bring patience for the first part of the trip. The bureacracy/registration will be a nightmare, and you're just gonna have to deal with with it.
- Travel as much as you can when you get the oppurtunity. Taiwan truly shines outside of its cities. You will love it, I promise. Its all the best and most interesting parts of Asia smashed together in a package where crime seemingly just does not exist.
- Bring more money than you think. Taiwan is cheaper than western Europe, but not eastern europe. Budget accordingly.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: You don't have to do Mandarin if you don't want to, but if you're staying here for 2 semesters, I think its a wonderful oppurtunity to learn a solid introduction to a very different language pretty comfortably. If you're only staying here for a semester, and you're starting from scratch, it may be limited how much you in practice may pick up, so plan accordingly.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people and the culture that I met along the way. Even though I really did just hang out with a lot of Germans for most of the trip, it was so wonderful to be away for so long and completely submerge myself in something that's so different from home, but still really so very, very nice.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I was pretty scared of the political situation, and I freaked out a little every time my roomie burned her rice and set off the fire alarm. Additionally, you will be very far from home, so holding onto family/friends/romantic relationships will be difficult across time-zones. Most manage to do it, but you will need to put some effort into it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I probably wouldn't go for the academics, and I definitely wouldn't go for the registration process, but if you want to experience one of the nicest parts of Asia, a little pearl of history, cross-cultural influences and burgeoning national identity, I can't recommend Taiwan enough.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
